2 | P a g e
Before : P. Kumaratnam, J.
Pradeep Hettiarachchi, J.
Counsel : Neranjan Jayasinghe with Randunu Heellage and Pravindika
Kularathne for the Accused-Appellant.
: Azard Navavi, ASG for the Respondent.
Argued on : 18-06-2026
Decided on : 21-09-2026
Pradeep Hettiarachchi, J
Judgment
1. This appeal arises from the judgment dated 04.01.2024, delivered by the Learned High
Court Judge of Colombo. The Accused-Appellant (hereinafter referred to as “the
Appellant”) was indicted before the High Court of Colombo in case No. HC 592/2018
on the following counts:
a. On or about 28.07.2016, within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Colombo,
the Accused was found in possession of 8.88 grams of Heroin without the
authority or a license as permitted by the Director in terms of Chapter 5 of the
Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 41 of
2022, an offence punishable under Section 54A (d) of the said Ordinance;
b. At the same time, during the same transaction, the Accused, by trafficking 8.88
grams of Heroin, committed an offence punishable under Section 54A (b) of the
Poisons, Opium and Dangerous Drugs Ordinance as amended by Act No. 41 of
2. At the trial, two witnesses testified for the prosecution. Since both parties admitted the
Government Analyst’s Report under Section 420 of the Code of Criminal Procedure
Act, it was marked as P10 in evidence through the High Court Interpreter. The
Appellant subsequently made a dock statement.
3 | P a g e
3. At the conclusion of the trial, the learned Trial Judge found the Appellant guilty of both
counts. The Appellant was accordingly convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment.
Aggrieved by the said conviction and sentence, the Appellant has preferred the present
appeal on the following grounds;
a. The learned High Court Judge had failed to take into consideration the serious
infirmities of the prosecution case; and
b. The learned High Court Judge had failed to evaluate the dock statement and
adduce reasons for his conclusion to reject the dock statement.
4. The first ground of appeal advanced by the Appellant was that the learned Trial Judge
failed to take into consideration the serious infirmities of the prosecution case. I shall
now consider whether such a contention is borne out by the judgment, in light of the
evidence adduced by the prosecution.
5. PW1, Wimalasena Lionel, was the first witness to testify on behalf of the prosecution.
At the material time, he was serving as an Inspector of Police attached to the Police
Narcotics Bureau. According to his evidence, at approximately 14.45 hours, he received
information from a private informant that a person known as ‘Niyas,’ residing at
Kajeema Watta, Ferguson Road, was engaged in the trafficking of Heroin and would be
proceeding towards the vicinity of the Weligoda Mosque carrying Heroin.
6. PW1 testified that, upon receipt of this information, he informed the Officer-in-Charge,
following which the officers of the Police Narcotic Bureau left the police station at
about 15.30 hours and proceeded towards Stadium Park, the car park near the
Sugathadasa Stadium. According to PW1, the informant met in the said car park. They
travelled in police jeep No. WPKP 5795, driven by PS Udayakumara 18314.
7. PW1 further testified that, prior to leaving the police station, he made the relevant out
entry in his notes at approximately 15.15 hours. Thereafter, they arrived at Stadium
Park at about 15.55 hours and met the informant at about 16.20 hours. According to
PW1. The informant informed them that the Appellant would be arriving in the vicinity
of the mosque between 5.00 p.m. and 5.30 p.m.
4 | P a g e
8. Thereafter, PW1 and PS Sanjeewa 60728 (PW4), accompanied by the informant,
proceeded towards the mosque and sat on a small wall situated near a playground in the
vicinity of the mosque. The other members of the police team were instructed to remain
near the Madampitiya Cemetery.
9. According to the witness, while they were seated there, the informant identified the
Appellant, who was approaching them accompanied by another person wearing a grey-
coloured striped T-shirt and grey-coloured denim trousers. Then, PW1 and PW4
proceeded towards the Appellant and conducted a search. During the search, a quantity
of Heroin was found concealed in a pink-coloured grocery bag kept in the right-side
pocket of the Appellant’s trousers. PW1 thereafter arrested the Appellant at about 17.40
hours, after informing him of the offence for which he was being arrested.
10. PW4 also proceeded to arrest the other person who had accompanied the Appellant.
However, nothing incriminating was found in his possession; thereafter, PW1 and PW4,
together with the Appellant and the other person who had been arrested, proceeded in
the said police jeep to the vicinity of the Madampitiya Cemetery, where an inquiry was
conducted. During the course of the inquiry, it was revealed that the Heroin had
allegedly been obtained by the Appellant from his brother-in-law, who was residing in
Wattala. Prior to proceeding from the Madampitiya Cemetery towards Wattala, PW1
handed over the parcel containing the Heroin and the other items recovered from the
Appellant to PW4. The police team thereafter proceeded to Wattala with the Appellant
and took his brother-in-law into custody.
11. Then, the police team subsequently returned to the Police Narcotics Bureau at about
21.15 hours. Thereafter, the parcel containing the Heroin was sealed and handed over
to PC Keerthi on 29.07.2016 at 7.15 hours. In the meantime, the production had been
kept in the private locker of PW1 until it was handed over to the receiving officer.
12. The next witness called on behalf of the prosecution was PW14, Keerthi Perera.
According to his evidence, he received the production relating to the Appellant from
PW1 on 29.07.2016 at 7.17 hours. Further, he testified that he subsequently handed
over the said production to the Government Analyst’s Department on 01.08.2016 at
10.40 hours.
5 | P a g e
13. The next material witness called by the prosecution was PW4, Prasad Sanjeeewa.
According to his testimony, upon the instructions of PW1, he accompanied the police
team to the location for the purpose of conducting the raid. PW4 testified that, after
arriving at the said ground, they remained there waiting for approximately one hour.
However, this evidence is materially inconsistent with the evidence of PW1 as to the
period during which they remained in the vicinity of the ground awaiting the Appellant.
“ප්‍ර: මහත්මයලා ඔය ස්ථානයේ ඔය ය ාරතුරුකරුත් එක්ක යකාච්චර යෙලාෙක් හිටියද
ගිහිල්ල?
උ: සාමානයයයන් පැයකට අසන්න කාලයක් ස්ොමිනි.” (at vide pages 203-204 of the
Appeal Brief)
14. Another inconsistency between the evidence of PW1 and PW4 relates to the location
of the premises where the alleged raid was conducted. PW1 testified that the car park
known as ‘Stadium Park’ was situated behind the Sugathadasa Stadium. In contrast,
PW4, when questioned regarding the location to which they left for the raid, stated that
it was situated in the Keththarama area. Thus, the evidence of PW1 and PW4 is
inconsistent as to the precise location of the said car park where the police team
allegedly proceeded prior to the raid.
“ප්‍ර: ඔය මහත්මය ස්යේ ඩියම් පාර්කක් කියල හදුන්ෙන පාර්කක් එක මහත්මය මත්රෙය නාශක
කාර්කයාාංශයේ ඉදල යකාච්චර ෙයේ දුරකින්ද තියෙන්යන්?
උ: සාමානය දුර ප්‍රමාණයක් තියෙනො. යකත් ාරාම ප්‍රයේශයේ පිහිටලා තියෙන්යන්.” (at
vide page 196 of the Appeal Brief)
15. There is further discrepancy between the evidence of PW1 and PW4 regarding the time
at which the Appellant was taken into custody. PW1 testified that the Appellant was
taken into custody at 17.40 hours, whereas PW4 testified that the Appellant was taken
into custody at 14.40 hours. This discrepancy concerns a material aspect of the
prosecution case as to the time at which the Appellant was allegedly apprehended.
“ප්‍ර: එය ායකාට දැන් මහත්මය ඔය ය ාරතුයර්ක ය ාරතුරුකරු කියපු ආකාරයට මහත්මය
හදුනායෙන යහයරායින් සන් කයේ තිබුණු පුේෙලයා සම්ෙන්ධෙ යමාකද කයල්?
යහයරායින් යසායා ෙත් ට පස්යස්?
6 | P a g e
උ: අාංක 233/142/බි යහ්නමුල්ල කදවුර, මාදම්පිටිය පර, යකාළඹ 15 ලිපිනයේ පදාංචි
යමායහාමඩ් නියාස් යමායහාමඩ් උදුර්කදන් යන අය යහයරායින් ලෙ ො ෙැනීයම් ෙරද කියා
දීලා පැය 14.40 ට පමණ ලයනල් මහ ා විසින් අත්අඩාංගුෙට යෙන ඔහුට අත් විලාංගු
යයදීමක් සිදු කලා ස්ොමිනි.” (at vide pages 207-208 of the Appeal Brief)
16. A further inconsistency arises between the evidence of PW1 and PW4 regarding the
time at which they left the Police Narcotics Bureau. PW1 testified that he made the
relevant out entry at 15.15 hours and left the Police Narcotics Bureau at about 15.30
hours. In contrast, PW4 testified that he reported to the Police Narcotics Bureau at about
15.50 hours. This evidence is inconsistent with the prosecution version as to the time at
which the police team commenced its journey to the alleged raid.
“ප්‍ර: පැය කීයටද මහත්මයායේ පිටවීයම් සටහන යයදුයේ?
ප්‍ර: මහත්මයා පැය 15.15 ට පිටවීයම් සටහන යයාදල ස ය ෙශයයන්ම මත්රෙය නාශක
කාර්කයාාංශ භූමියයන් පිටත් වුයන් කීයටද?
උ: පැය 15.15 ට සටහන් යයාදල පහල ෙරාජයට ගිය. ඉන් අනතුරුෙ රථය පරික්ෂ
කිරීයමන් පසුෙ පැය 15.30 ට පහල ෙරාජයයන් පිටෙ ගිය.” (at vide page 82-83 of the
Appeal Brief)
“ප්‍ර: එය ායකාට මහත්මයා ලයනල් මහත්මයා විසින් මහත්මයට ලොදීපු නියයෝෙයට
අනුෙ මහත්මයා යමාකක්ද කරපු ක්‍රියාෙ?
උ: ඒ අනුෙ මා සිවිල් ඇදුමින් සැරසී ෙැටලීමකට යාම සදහා යචෝදනාොරයට පැය 15.50
පමණ ොර්ක ා කලා.” (at vide page 193 of the Appeal Brief)
17. It should further be noted that, according to the evidence of PW1 and PW4, the
informant was present with them at the time of the alleged raid. However, the presence
of the informant at the scene of the alleged raid is itself questionable, particularly in
view of the circumstances in which the raid was said to have been conducted.
“ප්‍ර: ඒ අෙස්ථාෙ ෙන විට ඔය ය ාරතුරුකරු යකායහද හිටියේ මහත්මය?
උ: අපිත් සමෙයි රැදී සිටියේ.” (at vide page 89 of the Appeal Brief)
7 | P a g e
18. These unexplained omissions and inconsistencies in the evidence of PW1 and PW4
raise serious doubts regarding the integrity of the investigation. The cumulative effect
of the aforementioned contradictions in the evidence of PW1 and PW4 substantially
undermines the credibility of the prosecution case. Their inconsistent statements
regarding the place at which they met the informant, and the time of the Appellant’s
arrest, create serious doubt as to the reliability of the prosecution version.
19. These are not minor discrepancies but go to the root of the prosecution’s case,
particularly in relation to the time and place of the arrest. In a case of this nature, where
the prosecution’s case rests predominantly on the evidence of police officers, it is
imperative that such evidence be clear, consistent, and free from material
contradictions. The failure to meet this standard renders it unsafe to place reliance on
the testimonies of PW1 and PW4, thereby entitling the Appellant to the benefit of a
reasonable doubt.
20. Owing to the contradictory nature of the prosecution evidence, a reasonable doubt arises
regarding the time and place of the arrest, and the manner in which the raid was
allegedly conducted. Moreover, these inconsistencies directly undermine the credibility
of PW1 and PW4, as the discrepancies in their evidence have not been sufficiently
explained and are difficult to justify. The following authorities illustrate the
consequences of the prosecution’s failure to establish the charges beyond a reasonable
doubt.
21. In Kalinga Premathilake vs. The Director General of the Commission to Investigate
Allegations of Bribery or Corruption, SC Appeal No. 99/2007, decided on 30-07-2009,
it was held,
“What needs consideration now is when the evidence led for the prosecution in this
case is closely scrutinized, whether it would be satisfied that the prosecution had
discharged the burden of proving the case beyond a reasonable doubt. If not, the
appellant is liable to be acquitted of the charges. The prosecution must stand or fall
on its own legs, and it cannot derive any strength from the weaknesses in the
defence, and when the guilt of the accused is not established beyond a reasonable
8 | P a g e
doubt, he is liable to be acquitted as a matter of right and not as a matter of grace
or favour.”
22. In Narendra Kumar vs. State (NCT of Delhi), AIR 2012 SC 2281, the Indian Supreme
Court held:
“Prosecution case has to stand on its own legs and cannot take support from the
weaknesses of the case of defence. However great the suspicion against the accused
and however strong the moral belief and conviction of the Court, unless the offence
of the accused is established beyond a reasonable doubt on the basis of legal
evidence and material on the record, he cannot be convicted for an offence. There
is an initial presumption of innocence of the accused, and the prosecution has to
bring home the offence against the accused by reliable evidence. The accused is
entitled to the benefit of every reasonable doubt.
23. It is also desirable to emphasize that the officers, when conducting a raid of this nature,
are required to make notes on every important event and are also entitled to peruse their
notes in order to refresh their memory when testifying. Hence, where material
contradictions are present in their testimony, the Court cannot lightly disregard such
inconsistencies and proceed to convict the Appellant.
24. Unfortunately, the aforesaid infirmities, together with the material inconsistencies in
the prosecution evidence, appear to have escaped the attention of the learned Trial
Judge.
“එයස්ම චුද පැමිණීමට යපර ෙැලියොඩ පල්ලිය ඉදරිපිට පැය භාෙයක පමණ කාලයක්
සිටි ෙෙ පැ. සා. 1 පෙසන කරුණත්, පැ. සා. 04 පයක පමණ කාලයක් සිටියේ යන කරුණත්
නඩුයේ හරයට ෙලපාන පරස්පර ාෙයක් යලස සැලකීමට හැකියාෙක් නැ .
මක්නිසාදත් යදයදනාම අසන්න යෙලාෙක් පෙසන අ ර එය නිශ්චි යනාෙන යහයිනි.
එයස්ම යමම කාලපරාසය ආසන්න ෙශයයන් පැය භාෙයක් ෙන අ ර කිසියෙකු
ඔරයලෝසුයේ නිශ්චි යෙලාෙක් සදහන් කර යනාමැති යහයින් යමය ෙැදෙත්
පරස්පර ාෙයක් යනායේ.” (at vide page 376 of the Appeal Brief)
25. Further, it was contended on behalf of the Appellant that the learned High Court Judge
failed to properly evaluate the dock statement of the Appellant. However, I shall not
9 | P a g e
consider this ground of appeal, as the above-mentioned ground of appeal is sufficient
to dispose of this appeal.
26. For the reasons set out above, the said infirmities discernible in the prosecution’s
evidence render the conviction unsafe and untenable.
27. Accordingly, the conviction and sentence dated are hereby set aside. The Appellant is
acquitted of all charges. The appeal is allowed.
Judge of the Court of Appeal
P. Kumararatnam, J.
I agree
Judge of the Court of Appeal
